articles.summary:
WhatsApp has officially restricted access for smartphones running outdated operating systems, requiring users to upgrade to Android 6.0 or iOS 15.5 to maintain connectivity on the messaging platform.

### Key Points
- WhatsApp implemented a server-side block that prevents users on unsupported legacy software from accessing the application.
- The platform now requires a minimum of Android 6.0 (Marshmallow) for Android devices and iOS 15.5 for Apple hardware.
- Older devices, including aging Samsung Galaxy models and early iPhone generations, are no longer compatible with the service.
- The enforcement is permanent, displaying a full-screen warning that cannot be bypassed until the device software is updated or replaced.
- WhatsApp cited cybersecurity risks, noting that legacy operating systems lack the security patches necessary to protect against modern malware and data interception.

### Why it Matters
This policy shift highlights the growing tension between maintaining legacy hardware and ensuring robust end-to-end encryption security. Users must now prioritize software lifecycle management to avoid sudden service disruptions and potential vulnerabilities associated with unpatched operating systems.

articles.title: Staying ahead of the Chicoms: Beijing’s semiconductor bottlenecks are fading away
articles.author: RealClearWire
articles.content:
Washington’s semiconductor debate increasingly centers on the question: Can China build an extreme ultraviolet lithography machine? EUV systems are essential for producing the world’s most advanced chips efficiently, and China still cannot manufacture them at scale. That constraint matters. But a strategy built around one machine risks missing the larger change underway across China’s semiconductor industry. Meanwhile, making smaller chips is increasingly less important to the future of advanced semiconductors as physics constraints slow progress and advanced packaging creates a new avenue for improvement.
Beijing is steadily reducing its dependence on foreign suppliers across the broader chip supply chain. That progress is uneven, and some critical gaps will remain for years. Still, the direction is clear. China is building domestic capabilities in the equipment, materials, components and manufacturing processes needed to support a far more self-sufficient semiconductor ecosystem. Missing that key point could become a major strategic setback for the Western tech ecosystem
Our review at Sinolytics examined 20 enabling technologies across the semiconductor supply chain. Three years ago, roughly 60 percent of those technologies were bottlenecks, meaning China lacked substantial domestic capabilities. Today, that share has fallen to about 40 percent. If current trends continue, it could decline to roughly 15 percent within the next three years. The figures are estimates rather than guarantees, but they show how quickly the industrial base is changing.
Photoresist offers a useful example. This light-sensitive material allows manufacturers to print circuit patterns onto semiconductor wafers. Foreign suppliers still provide roughly 92 percent of the photoresist used by China’s chipmakers, and Chinese producers remain especially weak in the most advanced grades. Yet one domestic supplier that began developing photoresist for immersion deep ultraviolet lithography in 2020 had reportedly qualified its product by late 2025 for use by leading chipmakers ChangXin Memory Technologies and Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation. As production increases, Chinese-made photoresist is likely to take a larger share of the domestic market.
China has also made gains in the equipment used to etch and deposit thin layers of material during fabrication. These tools become more important when manufacturers lack EUV and must repeat patterning steps to produce advanced chips. Shenzhen-based SiCarrier, which has close ties to Huawei, has emerged as an important domestic supplier. Its tools are supporting expanded production of advanced logic chips, while similar capabilities are becoming more important for memory manufacturing.
Serious constraints remain. Ion implantation and metrology are two of the hardest. China produces only a few dozen ion implanters each year and still depends heavily on imports. Of the 448 machines China imported in 2025, 306 came from the United States. The gap is largest in high-energy ion implanters used for production at 14 nanometers and below, where Chinese companies have not yet established mature alternatives. Metrology systems, which measure and inspect chips during production, present another durable challenge.
Domestic substitution also does not always eliminate foreign dependence. It often moves that dependence one step upstream. A Chinese equipment maker may replace a foreign machine while still relying on imported components, intermediate products or specialized materials.
Policymakers should therefore look beyond the nationality of the final supplier and map the full chain of inputs that makes production possible.
The policy implication is straightforward. Export controls are no longer able to provide a durable advantage against an industrial system designed to replace foreign technology. At most, restrictions may slow progress in selected areas for a limited period. They also intensify China’s incentive to develop substitutes, encourage Chinese customers to abandon foreign suppliers and reduce the revenue available for research and development by U.S. and allied companies. Continuing to treat controls as the centerpiece of strategy risks weakening the industrial base the United States needs to lead.
The United States should compete by widening its technological and commercial lead. That means expanding domestic production, supporting research, training workers, strengthening allied supply chains and keeping global markets open to trusted U.S. technology. Policymakers should track China’s progress across equipment, materials and upstream components so public investment follows the capabilities that matter most. Protecting national security requires specific safeguards for genuine military risks, not broad commercial restrictions that encourage faster localization.
China has not eliminated its semiconductor vulnerabilities. Yet those vulnerabilities are shrinking, and several may disappear faster than policymakers expect. Over the next five to ten years, China is likely to develop a highly localized semiconductor ecosystem that challenges international suppliers across many parts of the industry. The United States will need a faster rate of innovation and a stronger industrial base because regulation cannot freeze today’s supply chain in place.
Jost Wübbeke is Managing Partner at Sinolytics, a management consultancy focused on China. He is an expert on China’s industrial policy, supply chains, the automotive industry, and semiconductors. He advises board-level executives at multinational corporations and SMEs on navigating China’s political and business landscape amid growing geopolitical complexity. He holds a PhD on China’s industrial policy from the Free University of Berlin, was a research fellow at Tsinghua University, and studied International Relations and East Asian Economics in Berlin.
articles.summary:
China is rapidly reducing its reliance on foreign semiconductor technology by building domestic capabilities across its supply chain, challenging the long-term effectiveness of Western export control strategies.

### Key Points
- Sinolytics data shows the share of semiconductor technology bottlenecks in China dropped from 60% to 40% over the last three years.
- Domestic suppliers like SiCarrier are increasing production of etching and deposition tools to support advanced logic and memory chip manufacturing.
- Chinese photoresist producers have begun qualifying products for use by major firms like ChangXin Memory Technologies and Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation.
- China remains heavily dependent on imports for high-energy ion implanters and metrology systems, with 306 of 448 imported machines coming from the U.S. in 2025.
- Domestic substitution often shifts dependence upstream, as local equipment makers frequently rely on imported components and specialized materials.

### Why it Matters
- China’s accelerating industrial localization suggests that broad export controls are becoming less effective at maintaining a long-term technological advantage for the United States. Relying on these restrictions may inadvertently weaken the U.S. industrial base by reducing revenue for domestic research and development.

articles.title: Treasury crackdown exposes crypto's role in $2 million Hamas fundraising network
articles.author: Olivier Acuna
articles.content:
Treasury crackdown exposes crypto's role in $2 million Hamas fundraising network
The Treasury Department said the network raised more than $2 million through purported humanitarian charities, including hundreds of thousands of dollars sent in crypto.
- The U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned a Hamas military-wing member, two France-based individuals and two charities accused of helping raise more than $2 million for Hamas through cryptocurrency and purported humanitarian donations.
- Treasury said the network collected the funds between 2020 and 2026, including $1.5 million after Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, and sent hundreds of thousands of dollars in cryptocurrency to a Gaza-based Hamas commander.
- The sanctions freeze the designated parties’ assets under U.S. jurisdiction, generally bar Americans from doing business with them and expose foreign financial institutions facilitating significant transactions to potential penalties.
The U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned several parties in relation to the raising of over $2 million for Islamist militant group Hamas.
The Treasury designated a Hamas military-wing member, two France-based individuals and two charities it says helped move more than $2 million to Hamas through a sophisticated six-year fundraising operation that used cryptocurrency and purported humanitarian donations.
The department alleged that Faouzi Barika and Amel Oualid raised funds in France for humanitarian causes, then transferred it to Hamas, the group designated as a terrorist organization in numerous jurisdictions and which has governed the Gaza Strip since 2007.
The network collected more than $2 million between 2020 and 2026, including $1.5 million after Hamas’s Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel, Treasury said. It said the pair sent hundreds of thousands of dollars in crypto to al-Zaq. Treasury did not say the full $2 million moved in cryptocurrency. It separately alleged that Barika and Oualid sent hundreds of thousands of dollars in crypto to Saleem Abdallah Saleem al-Zaq, a Gaza-based deputy battalion commander in Hamas’s Al-Qassam Brigades.
The action is the latest indication that U.S. authorities are focusing on crypto’s role inside wider fundraising and payment networks, rather than portraying it as Hamas’s primary funding source. Treasury officials have previously said Hamas and other groups still rely mainly on conventional finance, despite previously already being levied crypto-related sanctions and seizures.
It also follows reports last month that the Al-Qassam Brigades advised donors to avoid sending funds directly from Binance and instead use other crypto services before moving money to a TRON wallet.
The new sanctions block any property or interests in property held by the designated people and organizations under U.S. jurisdiction. People in the United States are generally barred from transacting with them, while foreign financial institutions that knowingly facilitate significant transactions could face secondary sanctions risk. The restrictions also extend to companies owned 50% or more, directly or indirectly, by one or more designated parties.
“Terrorist organizations like Hamas rely on sophisticated financial facilitators and fraudulent schemes designed to exploit the public,” said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
As stablecoins move into regulated finance, APAC is becoming a key proving ground. This report maps the region’s rules, use cases, and RLUSD’s role.
Why it matters:
As stablecoins move into regulated finance, APAC is becoming a key proving ground. This report maps the region’s rules, use cases, and RLUSD’s role.
articles.summary:
The U.S. Treasury Department has sanctioned five individuals and entities for operating a fundraising network that funneled over $2 million to Hamas using cryptocurrency and fraudulent humanitarian charities.

### Key Points
- The Treasury sanctioned a Hamas military-wing member, two France-based individuals, and two charities for facilitating illegal financial transfers.
- The network raised more than $2 million between 2020 and 2026, with $1.5 million collected following the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
- Funds were moved through purported humanitarian efforts, with hundreds of thousands of dollars transferred via cryptocurrency to Gaza-based commander Saleem Abdallah Saleem al-Zaq.
- Sanctions freeze all assets under U.S. jurisdiction and prohibit Americans from conducting business with the designated parties.
- Foreign financial institutions that knowingly facilitate significant transactions for these entities now face potential secondary sanctions risk.

### Why it Matters
This action highlights the ongoing efforts by U.S. regulators to dismantle sophisticated financial networks that exploit digital assets to fund militant organizations. It underscores the government's strategy of targeting specific facilitators to disrupt terrorist financing while acknowledging that such groups continue to rely on a mix of conventional and crypto-based payment systems.

articles.title: Anthropic says its IPO could herald the end of the world as we know it
articles.author: Brandon Vigliarolo
articles.content:
Anthropic's IPO prospectus leaked this week, and boy was it filled with interesting details.
You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle on this page, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, or YouTube. You can also subscribe on those platforms to be notified when a new episode goes live
For starters there's the fact a third of it is all about existential AI risks, then there's the fact that, despite some impressive revenue growth the company still has yet to turn a profit. Combine that with massive capex predictions, and you have an IPO with massive valuation, yet a long, hard road toward anything resembling earnings. 
Join host Brandon Vigliarolo, El Reg editor in chief Matt Rosoff, and enterprise IT reporter Lindsay Clark on this week's episode of The Kettle where they discuss the revelations, what they mean for the state of the AI industry, and just how much distraction from its actual problems Anthropic can eke out by keeping that doomsday narrative front and center. 
A lightly edited transcript is below: 
Brandon (00:04)
Hi everyone, and welcome to another episode of The Register's Kettle podcast. I'm your host, Brandon Vigliarolo, and this week we're gathered around the teapot to discuss hey, what else, AI? Specifically, the reported leak of Anthropic's IPO prospectus, which was apparently filled with all the doom, gloom, and to the moon promises for investors you'd expect from the world's most disruptive industry. With me to talk about the revelations are our editor-in-chief Matt Rosoff and enterprise IT reporter Lindsay Clark who brought us news of this whole mess. Thank you both for joining me.
Lindsay Clark (00:36)
Thank you.
Matt Rosoff (00:37)
Thanks for having us.
Brandon (00:38)
Yeah. So Lindsay, I know we didn't break this story. This was, I believe, a Financial Times exclusive, but what was reported about those IPO docs, in the story you wrote and just how apocalyptically optimistic is this whole thing?
Lindsay Clark (00:53)
Well we have this scenario where a company, Anthropic, is trying to sell itself by telling people that there's an existential risk to its technology, which I think is a bit of a weird way to go about it. But nonetheless, that's in the prospectus according to the Financial Times. And they also offer some insight into the numbers that are going around. Anthropic is still massively loss-making as far as we know.
Brandon (01:22)
There was what, I think you said, $8 billion loss on $4.6 billion of [revenue] or something? 
Lindsay Clark (01:28)
That's right, and it says it plans to spend $500 billion or so on cloud computing over the next few years. So I don't know what you make of those numbers, but it's hard to get them to add up in my head.
Brandon (01:40)
I mean it's interesting just how it's still not a profitable company. But Matt and I were discussing earlier, I was saying that I think it's interesting that Anthropic is pushed ahead with this IPO despite OpenAI pausing it, because I feel like Anthropic has long had this reputation as sort of being the more safety-conscious, the more conservative AI company. But here they are with OpenAI kind of saying, Well, we're gonna pump the brakes on our IPO until we can make sure our models are safe, but Anthropic is plowing ahead. And Matt, you had an interesting take on that and it was more to the financial end, right? So what were you saying to me about that earlier?
Matt Rosoff (02:21)
I think that if you probably were to look at OpenAI's numbers, they would be even worse than Anthropic's. And I can't overstate based on the leaked prospectus information that we've seen. It seems as if the more money they earn, the more they have to spend. So the margins seem pretty bad. Now there was a report that they had actually turned profitable on an adjusted basis [in] Q2 this year, but that's if you strip out all of the training costs. So I guess if it's just inference alone, without the training costs and without certain other costs, they have decent margins. So maybe there is a path to profitability.
Now it looks as if their operating loss last year was almost double their revenue. So if their revenue continues to increase at the rate that it is, which is, it seems like it's going up 4x, 12x per year, something like that, depending on the period you're looking at. If they can't get the expenses under control, the business doesn't seem to make a whole lot of sense.
Nonetheless, I think they are growing faster because they were earlier to enterprise and they have become more essential to more companies than OpenAI did. And I think OpenAI is still sort of adjusting its business model and maybe not growing at quite the same rate. So that's my suspicion is that those numbers would look even worse.
Brandon (04:01)
Yeah, so the safety argument is probably just some spackle slapped on top of the bad financials to try to kinda hide it, I guess. If what you're saying is correct.
Matt Rosoff (04:12)
That's my speculation. It doesn't seem to make a whole lot of sense to say, well, we're so worried about this amazing thing that we've built that we don't want to show you our books and we're not gonna go public yet until we have that all figured out. That seems like a strange argument to make.
Brandon (04:31)
Yeah, I would have to agree with that. So speaking of economic impact, Lindsay, you were talking a bit more in your story about some of the broader sort of economic scope of the AI industry. And I'm curious, could you go more into some of the numbers you discussed in your story?
Lindsay Clark (04:51)
Yeah, sure. So it was a few months ago, I think in August, ING. Well, I'll go back a bit. So in 2025, there was an economist, Jason Furman, who estimated that 92% of the US GDP growth in the second half of 2025 was down to AI investment. Now that figure has come down, ING said in August it was about a third and I've just seen a more recent figure saying it's about a fifth. So, nonetheless, a lot of US growth is coming from AI spending and I mean the forecast for spending, there's one estimate from Bain, capex on AI datacenters will be 6 trillion by 2031. And then PWC said capex again would be 31 trillion or so by 2050. So God knows what will be happening by 2050, but a lot of money spent on datacenters according to PWC.
Matt Rosoff (06:03)
What's not clear to me is where is all this money going to come from? Where do you find $31 trillion to subsidize what is still essentially a loss-making industry?
Brandon (06:15)
Right.
Lindsay Clark (06:16)
This is the trillion-dollar question, if you excuse me. I spoke to Gartner earlier this year and Gartner is still very optimistic about AI and tech spending. Most of the tech spending is coming from AI investment by tech companies, so about two thirds of the total tech spending in the world is coming from tech companies themselves investing in AI. Surely that must be passed on in some way to tech companies' customers. And that's true, a lot of these models will be embedded in the applications and the products businesses use. What concerns me and what is an open question at the moment, I think, is we're seeing cheaper models flood into the market. Open source, open weight models and kind of commoditized models from China. And everyone I speak to in development, datacenter companies, which is my beat, say that internally, they're completely trying to cut costs by using cheaper models wherever they can and not going to the most expensive model first, as it were. And yet these AI companies we've just mentioned, they're ploughing billions and billions of dollars into building bigger and better models. I don't know how OpenAI and Anthropic, how their forecasts depend on still being able to charge top dollar to access their models if the market is going to commoditize very quickly. 
Brandon (08:01)
Right. I mean, it's most business use cases don't even require these models, right? You can make do with a smaller local model. I mean, it's interesting, right? We saw with the whole Jev boom recently. A lot of business AI uses can be done by these decision models, right? You don't need a full LLM doing all this stuff. And, Jev was already what 0.042 cents per million tokens going in and free going out? And then Cloudflare just comes out with an open weight version that can be installed on local hardware. If you run it on their hardware, it's a bit more expensive thinking by a factor of six, which is still cheap, right? But it's available on Hugging Face, and they're like, if you got the hardware to run it, go ahead and download it and run it yourself. Right. It's like there's a lot of ways to trim AI costs. And I think the pipeline for these big companies is....I don't know if it's super clear, right? They're banking on a lot of what-ifs to hit profitability.
Matt Rosoff (09:03)
Right. I think probably the idea Anthropic had is that they will subsidize the costs initially, get enterprises hooked on the product, and then gradually raise prices when companies don't really have an alternative. But they do have alternatives and I think that's probably something they hadn't anticipated working out quite the way that it did.
Brandon (09:24)
That's probably why Deepseek was such a bomb in the industry when it first came out, earlier this year, right? Everyone was like, Well, the age of Anthropic and OpenAI is over if these are what these open weight models can do. And it doesn't seem like it's gotten a lot better, right? And now we're staring down the barrel of this massive percentage of the American economy being dedicated to this. I mean, Lindsay, you mentioned in your story that it was comparable in a lot of ways to the dot com boom, but maybe hyper inflated. And so do you have any idea relative to the dot com boom what kind of economic impact this could have on the global economy? Like what share of the economy is tied up in AI investment right now versus dot com?
Lindsay Clark (10:06)
 I don't have a direct comparison. It's worth remembering that although the dot com boom and subsequent crash, billions and billions of dollars were wiped off the stock market value, the actual real economy recovered quite quickly from that. Contained within the tech industry, there was a huge write off of telecoms investments. So a lot of telecoms companies put fiber in the ground. They were very leveraged to do that, financed by debt. And then the demand was not there as soon as they thought, and they were unable to service the debt. And a lot of these companies went bankrupt. They invested about $500 billion in that period. So that's the story there. And there was a real effect of the dot com crash. In some ways there was a technical recession and we weren't going great guns in the way we had done in the late '90s. But the effect on the real economy was not all that dramatic and the crash was relatively contained within the tech sector. And you have to remember that investment, that telecoms investment is being used eventually. It was used eventually. It was worth putting in the ground. It's just a lot of companies went bust in the meantime.
Brandon (11:34)
I guess which begs the question whether or not all these datacenters will end up being used if the AI bubble bursts, right? I got a feeling that maybe not. Maybe there'll be some massive redistribution of hardware.
Lindsay Clark (11:44)
I think in the long term, yes, but it just depends if the same thing happens In the meantime, a bunch of companies go bust. I mean, the thing that would concern me is how much of these circular investment strategies are going on where you see OpenAI is promising money to Oracle, but $300 billion to Oracle to build datacenters, but OpenAI doesn't have the money yet and this whole thing becomes quite circular. There's a number of these deals which are dependent on stock market price and so on.
Brandon (12:18)
Yeah, it's a real potential mess. Speaking of Oracle, right? I think you mentioned in your story that they're having some issues getting financing together for this New Mexico data center. And I think after you published that, it's come out in the past couple of days that they're also having similar problems at a Wisconsin facility they're trying to build. I know a lot of people were saying that Oracle might be the canary in the coal mine for all of this. 
Lindsay Clark (12:43)
Kind of yes and no. It's worrying. Oracle seems to be borrowing a lot of money. And I don't know if they're borrowing more than the other companies. I know Meta's borrowing as well. It's all to do with getting regulatory clearance for the power that goes into these data centers. That's why the force majeure was issued with the New Mexico data center to do with the developer.
Brandon (13:09)
Okay, so it has more to do with utility issues...
Lindsay Clark (13:12)
Yeah, but it shows the practicality of actually going from, hey, let's build a load of data centers to actually turning them on. I mean, can take longer than certainly longer than Oracle thinks.
Matt Rosoff (13:23)
Right, it's very easy to write in a prospectus or to say, "We're gonna build a bunch of data centers." It's much harder to do it. It's the sighting and the power and the other resources that need to be used and getting enough GPUs to put them in and letting the advanced networking technology to reduce latency. It's an incredibly complicated thing to do that is just sort of glossed over. We're gonna build some data centers. I mean these are orders of magnitude bigger than the ones that we were building twenty years ago to sort of power the first big generation of the internet. It's non trivial.
Brandon (14:01)
Yeah, no, absolutely.
Lindsay Clark (14:01)
Yes, I would agree with that. Although Oracle to some extent is writing this in Red Ink, its capex forecasts exceed its revenue for next year. Oracle has very deep pockets. It's got a huge number of enterprise customers that can't walk away from that software anytime soon. And so it has this cash cow of enterprise licenses that it will carry on milking for years to come. So it has very secure revenue streams. I'd hate to be the one to predict anything too bad happening to Oracle.
Matt Rosoff (14:36)
If anything, they can probably withdraw from some of these commitments and their core business will be fine. And that's the other thing. Google is doing a lot of build-out, Meta is doing a lot of build-out. These companies have an incredibly strong bottom line with huge, huge, huge margins. So to some degree, this is an affordable expense for some of them. It's just at some point the borrowing gets ahead of the revenue to a point where I wonder if some lenders will start to call debts in and that's when things can reverse in an interesting way.
Brandon (15:12)
Yeah, and for Meta and Google, right, and even Oracle, as you said, Lindsay, that might not be as big a problem, right? Because they have other things to fall back on. For OpenAI and Anthropic, on the other hand, where their entire business is based around AI buildouts, they don't have an alternative product to pull money from, redirect some funds. It's all kind of dependent on this. 
It's also interesting. Lindsay, when I was reading your story, I think it came out before that whole meeting that the Trump administration had with AI leaders this week. And we write a lot, and as you alluded to in your story, we write a lot about the fear-mongering around AI, right? About how this is all maybe just one big marketing ploy. It's a regulatory capture push. And I found it interesting that one of the sort of big headlines that made it out of there, aside from this voluntary AI pledge that is probably going to mean absolutely nothing, was the fact that a lot of these leaders in these meetings were really kind of laying into Dario Amodei for sounding the alarm on all this, right? Like they seemed upset that he was so aggressive on the apocalyptic warnings. What is that? I mean, what do you guys think that means for the AI industry? Are they all less scared than they let on? You know, is Amodei really pushing that hard to the point where it's become a joke kind of amongst people following this? What does it mean for the industry?
Matt Rosoff (16:38)
I sort of vacillate back and forth between "do they really believe this stuff" and "is this just a cynical marketing ploy"? Because what a great way to say, hey, this company is worth more out of the gate than any other IPO in history. It's a two trillion dollar value, but it's absolutely world-changing. It's akin to the invention or the discovery of fire or electricity or something like that. If you believe that, then that valuation is justified. And one way to get people to believe that is to say, this thing is so powerful, we don't even know what it can do. It's out of our control. It takes action on its own. There are internal documents and there's stories that leak about how people within Anthropic actually seem to refer to Claude as an independent living entity. There was a story in the New York Times recently about them consulting with religious leaders, asking for some guidance on how to make Claude act ethically, and in some of these conversations they were hinting that they thought that perhaps Claude might be an entity that is alive. I mean, this stuff is really fringy. 
So I had been in the camp that I thought it was kind of a cynical marketing ploy, but I'm not as sure. There was an article in the Wall Street Journal, I think this week, about sort of the history of where Amodei comes from and he comes out of the effective altruism movement, which is, in my opinion – 
Brandon (18:23)
Oh boy.
Matt Rosoff (18:24)
– a sort of fringe philosophy based on doing the most good for the most number of people in some sort of indeterminate long term future. And as I read about it, a lot of times it comes across as a convenient excuse for sociopathy, right? You can say, well, I can take this horrible action now, but it's going to be justified by things that happen in the future. At any rate, apparently he and some other folks, adherents to this philosophy, were all living in a house in the Glen Park neighborhood of San Francisco, which is actually kind of near where I live, and talking about these kinds of things. And Sam Bankman-Fried, who later went on to found a crypto company and then went to prison for fraud was part of that same philosophy.
Brandon (19:14)
Yeah. I feel like he's been he's been kind of the poster child for effective altruism as sort of like a hey, this might not be too legitimate.
Matt Rosoff (19:22)
Yeah, Anthropic is kind of distancing itself from this philosophy. But if you read this article, they were all kind of traveling in these circles and having these sort of deep philosophical debates. And apocalypse came up frequently before AI had been invented. So if you're looking for the end of the world everywhere already, and then you discover this really interesting new way of making computer systems operate in somewhat unpredictable fashion and allowing them to self-improve, maybe you're gonna project your end-of-the-world fantasies onto this particular technology. So maybe they really do believe it. I'm actually not sure. I just think it's crazy, it's nonsense, and I think I find myself in rare agreement with President Trump who sort of seems to be saying this is silly, stop talking like this, we have to continue developing this full speed ahead. 
Brandon (20:24)
Yeah.
Matt Rosoff (20:25)
I don't know if I believe that either. It does seem like we need to look at the very real safety effects and really very real things that are happening today and why some of these models are not in control and how guardrails can be placed on them and so forth. But to sort of have this, "It's gonna end the world and there's nothing we can do about it" is a really strange way of going about things.
Brandon (20:47)
Yeah, it is, especially when these companies are all the ones that really control the off switch, right?
Matt Rosoff (20:54)
Yeah.
Brandon (20:54)
I don't think we've had any AI models yet escape from their confines and replicate themselves somewhere on some mystery server that stays on no matter what happens. It's all perfectly within our control, right? The most critical systems in the government are air gapped. They probably can't be accessed by these things, right? Like I think there's some very real risk here too, right? Like we've seen some of the bad things these AI can do when you prompt them. Again, when you remove their guardrails and you give them problems that they cannot solve based on their own constraints, they're going to solve those problems and figure out a way to do it outside their constraints, right? They can act autonomously in bad ways to a degree. But I think going from that to, well, you might as well give us all the money you can so we can stop this thing from ending the world. It's just I don't see how A turns into B here, really.
Matt Rosoff (21:49)
Yeah.
Lindsay Clark (21:49)
And it's kind of a smoke screen for the nitty gritty, practical legislation that would be required to ensure companies take responsibilities for the technologies they've produced. And I've written about liability in using AI agents in business. And it's a completely unknown. The lawyers I spoke to said, we're just going to have to rely on test cases as they come through, certainly in Europe. The European Union's trying to introduce, well has introduced, legislation on AI. In the US not so much. So I think the whole doom talk avoids that conversation, or at least puts it off, which is what they all want to do until the IPOs are out of way and the money's in their pocket.
Matt Rosoff (22:35)
Right. What if I'm using an AI and it does something unintended and causes harm, whose fault is that? Am I liable for the prompt I gave it or is the company that created it liable? Yeah. These are all really good, interesting real world today questions... we don't have to think about the apocalypse.
Brandon (22:53)
Yeah, I mean we need to be asking, or like I think we've written on more than one occasion, I think maybe Tom has written this in his stories about OpenAI's AI agents going rogue and stuff. It's like if a human did any of these things, we would hold them legally accountable. Like when are we going to start holding these companies legally accountable for basically putting the entire internet downrange of their tests and saying, Hey, let's see what we can get this thing to do. 
Lindsay Clark (23:18)

We saw the SpaceX IPO earlier this year and that core business of launching rockets and satellites particularly looks okay. the AI component of the business looked less good, but it was good enough that it went public and the stock is a little bit above where it debuted. articles.summary:
Anthropic’s leaked IPO prospectus reveals a company facing significant financial losses and massive capital expenditure requirements while heavily emphasizing existential AI risks to potential investors ahead of its public offering.

### Key Points
- Anthropic reported an operating loss nearly double its revenue, despite claims of adjusted profitability in the second quarter of 2024.
- The company projects approximately $500 billion in cloud computing spending over the next few years to support its AI infrastructure.
- Financial analysts suggest the focus on "doomsday" existential risks may serve as a marketing narrative to justify high valuations rather than addressing practical business liabilities.
- The IPO is expected to move forward this fall, even as competitors like OpenAI have reportedly paused their own public offering plans.
- Industry experts warn that the AI sector faces a potential bubble, with massive capital investment in data centers currently outpacing clear paths to long-term profitability.

### Why it Matters
The financial disclosures highlight a growing disconnect between the massive capital requirements of AI development and the actual revenue generated by these models. Investors must now weigh whether these companies can transition from loss-making research entities into sustainable businesses before the current wave of AI-driven market optimism fades.

articles.title: Here’s What Capcom Said About Using Generative AI In The RE Engine: ‘AI Is Not A Replacement For Humans’
articles.author: Alicia Haddick
articles.content:
On October 2, Capcom held an open conference event for engineers and the games industry where it divulged information on the direction it wishes to take the RE Engine moving forward, including specifying where it wishes to use AI and where it wishes to avoid its use as the industry increasingly embraces the technology.
Over the last decade, Capcom has utilized its internally developed RE Engine on almost all of its projects, with the tools being optimized to allow for shared development knowledge across all teams at the company and to support the scaling of projects more easily to hardware of varying power, from PC to Nintendo Switch. Many say the technology is a key aspect of the company’s recent change in fortunes. At the conference, representatives from Capcom sought to discuss where the technology will continue to evolve, while sharing lessons they’ve learned from its development.
According to a report on the talk from GameBiz, the continued evolution and improvement of the RE Engine forms part of the REX Initiative (standing for RE neXt engine), first discussed by the company in 2023. These efforts are centered on five goals, including reducing complex code into simpler rules that the engine can process more quickly (RE:Dox) and generating more efficient and easier-to-modify internal reports for catching and amending errors in coding or compilation (RE:Log), among others. These all concern the kind of behind-the-scenes technology that most players will never need to worry about, but they’re designed to assist the engine’s ability to perform well on a range of different hardware.
The company, however, has insisted that part of the gradual improvement and evolution of the RE Engine is in service of developing an “engine for the AI generation” that will allow the company to “develop games together with AI.” Earlier this year, Capcom publicly assured audiences that its games would not include AI-generated assets and that its flirtations with AI were instead focused on improving efficiency during the development process.
As part of this evolving RE Engine, Capcom has chosen to release the RE:Dox and RE:Log tools as open-source tools on programming website Github. According to the company, by making these tools available online, it’s enabling AI programs to learn about the way they function. The hope is that, if AI can understand the tools, it will be able to look at human-developed code made internally at Capcom and assist in creating internal playtests of levels, searching for and fixing bugs.
According to one slide in the company’s presentation, these new AI agents will be able to play builds, log issues, analyze data, and detect visual and gameplay bugs and issues with memory or performance, then suggest a fix that a human developer would manually implement.
This is something a number of companies have been experimenting with for a number of years, even before generative AI was a major point of discussion for many studios. Notably, Sony previously discussed a similar concept a similar concept at Japanese developer conference CEDEC in 2024.
 #RE2026CAPCOM

And Capcom insists that this is the extent to which it seeks to implement AI in the process of game development. By using AI to limit the amount of repetitive work that human beings have to do, the hope is that those human developers can focus on the creative aspects of development. “AI is not a replacement for humans,” the company insisted during the conference.

### Key Points

- The company released its RE:Dox and RE:Log tools as open-source software on GitHub to facilitate AI-assisted development.

By automating bug detection and code maintenance, Capcom aims to increase development efficiency and allow human staff to prioritize creative design.

articles.title: Proposed anti-Flock bills could spell trouble for license plate readers
articles.author: Pieter Arntz
articles.content:
Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are cameras that photograph passing vehicles, read their number plates, and typically log the time, location, and vehicle details. On their own, the images might be used to find a stolen car or locate a suspect.
But lately there have been a lot of concerns raised about the way they are used. The main worry is caused by what happens when many cameras feed data into a shared, searchable network: it can create a detailed record of where ordinary people travel.
Some agencies have already taken it upon themselves to act on these concerns, as well as those around inaccuracy. Data errors can have serious consequences. At a recent Senate hearing, Florida resident Lindsey Isaacs described being arrested and held for 13 days after data from an AI-enabled plate-reader system incorrectly implicated her in a fatal car crash.
As a result of all this, US lawmakers from both major political parties have introduced proposals aimed at restricting automatic license plate reader networks.
Most of the reasons brought up are about Flock Safety, one of the largest suppliers of these systems in the United States, but they would apply more broadly to other ALPR vendors as well.
Flock says it deploys only 120,000 cameras operating across the country, while a researcher cited by the Senate described a much larger network of connected devices and cameras. The exact size may be disputed, but the central concern is clear: Data from a camera in one location can potentially be searched by an agency elsewhere.
Two different approaches
Reportedly, there are two different proposed laws in the making, while Flock says it supports a legal framework for license-plate readers and argues that the technology can improve public safety when it is used with strong oversight and accountability.
The first proposal, the Stop Flock Abuse Act, doesn’t aim to banish ALPR systems outright, it would create rules for how government agencies and vendors can use them.
Among other measures, the bill would require written approval and a record for every search, regular supervisor audits, encryption, and deletion of most vehicle-location data after ten days. It would also prohibit sharing or selling the data to non-governmental third parties, prevent ALPR networks from incorporating facial-recognition technology, and require data to stay in the US.
A second proposal, the Ban Flock Act, takes a much harder line. It would prohibit US federal agencies from using ALPRs or accessing data they collect. It would also withhold federal grant money from state and local governments that use ALPR systems and allow people to sue the federal government if their rights are violated through ALPR deployment.
Both bills are proposals, not enacted laws. In the US system, each would need to pass both the House of Representatives and the Senate in matching form, then be signed by the President.
Going forward
There is no guarantee either bill will receive a vote, let alone become law. But their introduction shows that ALPR technology is moving from a local procurement issue to a national privacy and civil-liberties debate.
License plate data may seem less sensitive than phone-location data, but a long enough record can reveal a person’s routines, relationships, medical visits, religious activity, or attendance at protests. The debate is therefore not just about cameras on streets to fight crime and find criminals, it is about whether governments and private vendors should be able to build searchable records of everyday movement.
So for consumers, the key question is not only whether a camera is installed on a street or near a business. It is also how long the resulting data is retained, who can search it, whether those searches are logged and reviewed, whether the information can be shared beyond the original agency, and what recourse exists when the system is wrong or abused.

articles.title: Interdependence and Its Limits | Sinification: September 2026
articles.author: James Farquharson
articles.content:
This monthly report is prepared for Sinocism by the excellent Sinification, an invaluable resource for understanding how domestic and international affairs are debated within the Chinese establishment. Thomas des Garets Geddes, will be in DC from 18–21 October and New York from 21–24 October. If you’re interested in Sinification’s work, would like to support it, or know someone Thomas should be speaking with, please do get in touch with him. They have several new research initiatives underway that are well worth hearing about. — Bill
Much of the commentary in September revolved around the strength and limitations of economic interdependence as a source of political power. Against the backdrop of “strategic stability”—or stalemate—in the US-China trade relationship, Wu Bingxuan and Huang Chaofeng advise Chinese firms to concentrate on trade diversification and developing sanctions-evasion tools against the prospect of expanding US trade controls and restrictions on Chinese firms.
Regarding the absence of a business delegation accompanying Xi to Washington for the summit last month, the well-connected political commentator “Chairman Rabbit” suggests China’s feelings of insecurity about the trading relationship may lie behind it. The presence of high profile Chinese CEOs could have invited scrutiny of their relationship with the state, or requests from Trump for them to invest in the US.
China-EU trade talks are ongoing, with a resolution hoped to be achieved by mid-October and a further escalation in trade tensions looming if the talks fail to deliver. While these talks take place, China’s global trade relationships are also in the spotlight elsewhere.
The “China squeeze” thesis, recently advanced by Arvind Subramanian and Shoumitro Chatterjee, continues to provoke indignation in China against the backdrop of Xi’s visit to New Delhi for last month’s BRICS summit. The economist Xia Chun rebuts the idea that China’s economic juggernaut is displacing industrial activity in developing countries, offering as he does so an interesting window into how many in China view the source of their industrial advantage. Liu Zongyi links the “China squeeze” concept to Indian policy circles and an attempt by New Delhi to compete with China for leadership over the Global South, while Jin Canrong advises Chinese enterprises to be cautious about investing in India.
Brazil, another Global South heavyweight, is already a rapidly growing destination for Chinese enterprises escaping the low-profit squeeze of race-to-the-bottom competition at home. Against the backdrop of the election race between Flavio Bolsonaro and Lula, several scholars look at how economic penetration and political influence interact. Li Wei observes that there is a mismatch between Brazil’s apparently “laid-back” approach to international affairs and the hope among some Chinese scholars that it could form a counterweight to the US in the western hemisphere.
Di Dongsheng and Zhao Yixian offer nicely contrasting prescriptions for Chinese businesses expanding their operations in Brazil. For Di, the goal should be to deepen Chinese influence in order to shift Brazil’s political and business climate in ways more favourable to Chinese firms. Zhao, meanwhile, suggests Chinese businesses expanding overseas should aim to build “a Brazilian company with Chinese strengths”, adapting to local requirements and labour practices from the outset. BYD, in particular, has drawn fire for its labour standards in the country.
On the domestic front, Yang Wenhui and Wu Xinye express thoughtful caution on the limitations of AI as a tool for improving governance, while a roundtable with some of China’s most influential economists sets out the main lines of debate over economic rebalancing and stimulus in China. Liu Shangxi, however, observes that beyond shuffling money around, resolving problematic moral hazard in China’s economy will require more thorough institutional reforms.
— James Farquharson
In Brief
- US-China: 
  - Meng Weizhan on the midterms and the durability of Trump’s accommodation with China
  - Liu Chong on developing a shared US-China vocabulary of AI risk
  - Wu Bingxuan & Huang Chaofeng on strategies for evading the expanding US sanctions toolkit
  - Ren Yi (Chairman Rabbit) on the possible reasons underlying the absent business delegation on Xi’s visit to Washington DC.
- Global Order: 
  - Zhu Zhaoyi on the need to better define China’s security role overseas.
  - Huang Ping on the challenge posed to certain middle powers’ leverage over AI supply chains by US–China accommodation
  - Sun Chenghao & Zhang Xueyu on how AI could drive more intense nuclear competition
  - Zhao Hongtu & Chen Wenlin on the rise of “electricity powers” and Europe’s energy dilemma
- Brazil: 
  - Li Wei on the gap between China’s commercial presence and America’s social influence in Brazil
  - Di Dongsheng on Chinese firms’ encounters with Brazil’s labour protections and development politics
  - Zhao Yixian on mitigating the risks faced by Chinese companies setting up operations in Brazil.
- India: 
  - Liu Zongyi on India’s BRICS ambitions and competitive coexistence with China
  - Jin Canrong advising caution to potential Chinese investors in India
  - Xia Chun on land reform, caste and the roots of China’s manufacturing lead over India
- Russia and North Korea: 
  - Li Shenghua & Wu Wenzhuo on the strategic implications of North Korea’s current leverage over Russia
- Economy: 
  - Ju Jiandong, Justin Yifu Lin, Yu Yongding, Yao Yang & Li Xunlei on China’s fiscal stimulus choices
  - Liu Shangxi on the obstacle posed by moral hazard to China’s economic transition
- AI and Tech: 
  - Yang Wenhui on how AI use could come into tension with local officials’ discretion and initiative
  - Wu Xinye & Wang Zice on how AI-assisted grassroots governance could simply amplify the loudest voices
  - Huang Rihan & Shi Yukun on the strategic purpose of US-China competition in orbital computing
- State and Society: 
  - Liu Yunshan on the issue of “exam specialists” among the younger generations
  - “Wen Ping” on algorithm-driven pseudo-history and upholding the correct national narrative
1. US-China
Meng Weizhan (孟维瞻): A narrow Democratic House majority would make Trump’s accommodation with China more politically costly, while leaving him substantial control over policy. Investigations, hearings and budget conditions could expose concessions to accusations of sacrificing national security for trade deals, and Democratic cooperation with Republican hawks over advanced chips, AI computing power, Taiwan and secondary sanctions could intensify this pressure. The main risk is that congressional pressure over export licences, sanctions and investment makes Trump’s existing accommodation with China harder to sustain, gradually eroding the summit’s stabilising effect. – Associate Research Fellow, Institute for Advanced Study in Social Sciences, Fudan University (Greater Bay Area Review, 28 September)
Liu Chong (刘冲): For a China-US cooperation framework on AI governance to succeed even as competition intensifies, a shared understanding of risk will be necessary first. The threshold for slowing or stopping AI training should depend less on a definition of whether AGI has been reached than on whether existing safeguards can reliably constrain a model. Governance standards should specify which combinations of capabilities warrant closer monitoring and what kind of abnormal behaviours warrant slower or suspended training. It may then be possible to establish scientific trust, mechanisms for sharing safety capabilities and a common understanding of when to apply the brakes. – Director, Centre for Technology and Strategy, China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations (CICIR, 28 September)
Wu Bingxuan (吴柄萱) & Huang Chaofeng (黄朝峰): The backdrop of stabilising US–China relations is not halting expanding financial restrictions on Chinese firms. Broader US trade controls require more diversified technology and supply chains, with risks assessed beforehand and alternative buyers and suppliers kept available. To counter tighter investment scrutiny, firms should expand de-dollarisation and use offshore financial centres and complex ownership structures to make transactions and acquisitions harder for US regulators to scrutinise. – Wu Bingxuan, PhD student, Koguan School of Law, Shanghai Jiaotong University; Huang Chaofeng, Professor and Deputy Director, National Institute for Strategic Studies, Shanghai Jiaotong University (Shanghai Jiaotong National Institute of Strategic Studies, 27 September)
Ren Yi (任意) / Chairman Rabbit : The absence of a full business delegation accompanying Xi to Washington may reflect concerns about sending the wrong policy signals domestically and internationally. Participation of Chinese companies in the delegation could mark private companies as state-linked targets for sanctions or distort domestic competition, or cause them to be pressured into US investments whose long-term security no White House administration can guarantee. Lower-profile exchanges through industry associations and state-level exchanges would allow greater economic cooperation while limiting these risks. – Political commentator (Tuzhuxi New Platform, 24 September)
2. Global Order
Zhu Zhaoyi (朱兆一): China’s Global Security Initiative needs to move from broad principles to practical security support. As Gulf states diversify their partnerships without giving up US deterrence, China could contribute crisis warning, mediation, shipping and energy security cooperation, humanitarian assistance and postwar reconstruction. This would give practical substance to “security governance without dependence” in the form of credible and lasting support at critical moments, without copying the US military alliance model or requiring countries to choose sides. – Executive director and associate professor, Middle East Institute, Peking University HSBC Business School think tank (contribution to a World Affairs roundtable, “The Paradox of Security Dependence”, 2026, Issue 18)
Huang Ping (黄平): The smaller economies that control critical AI technologies are indispensable to China and the US, giving them a degree of leverage that is nonetheless subject to the nature of the US-China relationship. These middle powers benefit most from a stable but limited Sino-US rivalry that preserves access to both markets: intensifying competition could force them to choose sides, while a US–China bargain could decide market outcomes without their participation. Following the summit, a shared interest in keeping East Asian semiconductor production running could further reduce the ability of these middle powers to gain leverage in the context of supply shortages. – Qianhai Institute for International Affairs (Greater Bay Area Review, 23 and 30 September).
Sun Chenghao (孙成昊) & Zhang Xueyu (张学玉): AI could intensify nuclear competition without an increase in warhead numbers. Better surveillance and targeting may threaten an adversary’s ability to retaliate, while gains from software and data remain hard to measure through arms control. Practical starting points would be to identify where AI enters nuclear systems and extend the US–China commitment to human control of nuclear weapons to all five recognised nuclear powers. – Associate Research Fellow, Center for International Security and Strategy, Tsinghua University; Research Assistant, Peking University (Strategic Decision-Making Studies, no. 5, 2026).
Zhao Hongtu (赵宏图) & Chen Wenlin (陈文林): The disruption of oil supplies during the US–Israeli conflict with Iran could accelerate the rise of “electricity powers”, especially in Asia. As countries seek to reduce their dependence on imported fuels and vulnerable shipping routes, influence will increasingly rest on the ability to manufacture and deploy clean-energy technology, alongside oil and gas reserves. Europe faces a dilemma: it wants faster electrification to improve energy security, but efforts to reduce dependence on external clean-energy supply chains raise costs and slow the transition. – Institute of Economic Research, China Institutes of Contemporary International Relations (Qiushi, no. 17, 1 September)
3. Brazil
Li Wei (李巍): Washington retains “social influence” in Brazil through regional elites’ children and assets in the US, enabling pressure through visa restrictions, while widespread admiration for America reinforces its influence. China’s extensive trade with Brazil has not yet translated into comparable geopolitical influence, and China should aim to deepen this partnership, exploring military cooperation to strengthen Brazilian autonomy and counterbalance US power. However, Brazil’s “laid-back” [佛系] approach to international affairs and limited ambition to become a global or military power mean that the prospect of Brazil playing a balancing role against the US is still distant. – Professor and Associate Dean, School of International Studies, Renmin University of China (Pingheng Xuehui, 23 September)
Di Dongsheng (翟东升): Chinese firms expanding into Brazil are often frustrated by cultural and institutional differences: labour protections prevent managers from pressing employees to work harder, while misguided progressive policies drain resources from Brazil’s industrial development. To strengthen and protect their investments in the country, Chinese firms should fund stronger industry associations to lobby governments, prevent involutionary competition from replicating overseas and pursue legal remedies when projects run into trouble. They should also work with Brazilian alumni of Chinese universities on cultural and scientific exchanges to build local influence and encourage Brazilians to draw lessons from China’s approach to development. – Dean, Institute of Area Studies, Renmin University of China (Guancha, 3 September)
Zhao Yixian (赵懿先): Chinese firms entering Brazil often choose the quickest, cheapest way to start operating and postpone building local compliance systems. These early decisions are a “slow poison”: tax, labour and other risks may emerge together three to five years later, when the business is larger and correction far more costly. Rather than rushing in, the goal should be to build “a Brazilian company with Chinese strengths”, capable of making decisions and sustaining relationships within Brazil’s institutions. – Director, Overseas Interests Protection Research Centre, East China University of Political Science and Law (Guancha interview, 8 September)
4. India
Liu Zongyi (刘宗义): India wants to use BRICS to strengthen its bargaining position with China and the West while avoiding a choice between them. It seeks to represent the Global South and act as its bridge to Western countries, without turning BRICS into an anti-Western bloc. Through the “China squeeze” narrative, India casts Chinese manufacturing dominance as a constraint on other developing economies in the Global South and gives India a basis to demand more Chinese investment and technology transfer. Its engagement with China thus forms part of a strategy of competitive coexistence, rather than alignment. – Director of the South Asia Research Centre at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies. (Guancha, 13 September)
Jin Canrong (金灿荣): Chinese businesses looking to invest in India should be cautious: India uses the promise of its vast market to attract Chinese businesses while imposing far tighter restrictions on China than China does on India. Chinese firms should prioritise exports over investment, insist on payment before shipment and favour projects with few fixed assets. If substantial investment is unavoidable, joint ventures with European or Russian firms in India would be an effective measure to spread the risk. – Professor, School of International Studies, Renmin University of China (WeChat Public Account, 7 September)
Xia Chun (夏春): The “China squeeze” thesis, advanced by two Indian economists to account for developing countries’ manufacturing difficulties, cannot explain China’s lead over India, which emerged before reform and opening in 1978. In comparison with India’s incomplete land reform, China’s land reform dismantled landlord power, weakened inherited status barriers and provided the fiscal basis for industrialisation. By contrast, India’s caste hierarchies restricted labour participation and its prioritisation of elite education did not create mass employment as with China’s industrialisation. Instead, India’s IT services attracted skilled workers and raised wage expectations, hindering manufacturing through a form of “Dutch disease”. – Founder and chief economist, Zhihui Group (New Economist, 3 September)
5. Russia and North Korea
Li Shenghua (李圣华) & Wu Wenzhuo (吴文茁): Russia currently depends more on North Korea than Pyongyang does on Moscow because it needs North Korean troops and weapons for the war in Ukraine. Pyongyang could turn this wartime leverage into longer-term gains through Russian economic and technological support and diplomatic backing, reducing its dependence on China. Russia’s need for the alliance could also draw it away from its longstanding opposition to North Korea’s nuclear programme and towards recognition of Pyongyang as a nuclear-armed state. – Professor, College of Economics and Management, and MA student, Centre for Korean Studies, Yanbian University (东疆学刊, 2026, issue 4)
6. Economy
Roundtable at the Tsinghua PBCSF Chief Economists Forum, 19 September: Ju Jiandong (鞠建东) recommends issuing renminbi government bonds overseas to support household incomes, replace local debt and fund investment while advancing renminbi internationalisation. Justin Yifu Lin (林毅夫) recommends central government assuming local debts incurred through implementing national policies, while leaving local governments responsible for vanity projects. Yu Yongding (余永定) urges stronger fiscal expansion and infrastructure investment to boost domestic demand, reduce trade surpluses and limit accumulation of risky dollar assets. Yao Yang (姚洋) supports borrowing domestically, where funds are abundant, and warns that long-term investment priorities cannot resolve immediate economic problems. Li Xunlei (李迅雷) recommends replacing local debt through recapitalisation measures, relaxing special-purpose bond spending restrictions and stimulating consumption to restore domestic economic circulation. (New Economist, 19 September)
Liu Shangxi (刘尚希): The issue of a “shared risk pot” [风险大锅饭] in China’s economy is allowing losses to be socialised through public finances and preventing markets from clearing risks. Implicit state guarantees make keeping inefficient businesses alive cheaper than restructuring, trapping resources in declining industries. Furthermore, an “information black hole” is undermining market-based risk pricing, making banks more cautious about lending and companies more hesitant to borrow. To reform this, capital costs should be made to reflect actual risks, bankruptcy procedures should be simplified to enable orderly exits and the allocation of responsibility within state-run sectors should be made clearer. – Vice-president, China Society of Macroeconomics and CPPCC National Committee member (People’s Political Consultative Daily, 7 September)
7. AI and Tech
Yang Wenhui (杨文辉): Excessive reliance on AI could undermine the discretion and initiative of local officials, which are both important sources of dynamism in China’s development and governance. AI tends to favour predictable and low-risk outcomes, potentially provoking the “passive resistance” of officials to AI adoption if they find reliance on the models constraining their freedom of action and creativity. AI adoption in government should therefore be concentrated in areas where rules are clear, data are abundant and the costs of error are low. Decisions requiring flexibility and ethical judgement should remain with human officials. – Assistant Professor, Institute of State Governance and School of Government, Peking University (E-Government, issue 8, 2026)
Wu Xinye (吴新叶) & Wang Zice (汪子策): While AI promises to improve grassroots governance in some respects, it could reinforce inequalities in whose needs are addressed. Digitally vocal groups could disproportionately influence resource allocation by officials, leaving less digitally engaged residents overlooked. AI systems gathering residents’ views may prioritise issues generating quick likes and comments, overlooking less popular problems that require sustained discussion. Offline outreach and face-to-face discussion should complement digital tools to counter such “click-based participation”. – Professor and PhD student respectively, School of Political Science and International Relations, Tongji University (Social Sciences, issue 8, 2026)
Huang Rihan (黄日涵) & Shi Yukun (石宇坤): Satellite computing constellations are an important field of development and geopolitical competition, potentially helping China maintain computing services when ground facilities and networks are disrupted. Furthermore, analysing satellite observations in orbit could speed disaster response by reducing the raw data that must reach Earth before action can be taken. Against the commercial model of SpaceX’s planned orbital data centres in the US, China’s state-led coordination could accelerate deployment despite the uncertain commercial returns. – Professor, School of International Relations, and PhD student, College of Foreign Languages, Huaqiao University (Contemporary International Relations, issue 8, 2026)
8. State and Society
Liu Yunshan (刘云杉): In China, the hope that education can change a family’s fortunes has, for some, turned the gaokao into a project that dictates a child’s entire school life. “Haidian mothers”, often first-generation university graduates, try to reproduce their success by preparing children for entry to prestigious universities. This can produce “exam specialists” skilled at finding high-scoring answers within fixed rules but less practised at solving uncertain problems. As marks and GPA become the currency of recognition, students often see themselves and others as occupying ranked positions in relation to each other. – Peking University Graduate School of Education (Educational Academic Monthly, 2026, no. 5)
“Wen Ping” (文平, pen name): Algorithm-driven “pseudo-history” threatens China’s cultural and ideological security by eroding historical understanding and national identity, particularly among young people. Claims that the Tang was a “foreign” regime, alongside narratives excluding the Yuan and Qing from Chinese history, link up with dangerous overseas narratives and undermine the historical consensus underpinning a unified, multiethnic Chinese nation. AI-generated false historical material, particularly from overseas, could enter training datasets, creating a feedback loop in which algorithms amplify biased narratives and reinforce distorted beliefs. Platforms must embed “mainstream values” in recommendation algorithms and act against accounts repeatedly spreading such claims. – (Qiushi, no. 17, 1 September)
Gung-Ho Diplomacy: Chinese Commentary on the Trump-Xi Summit (30 September)
In official commentary, symbolism and language are the focus, even if difficult questions lurk beneath. CCTV’s Yuyuan Tantian blog approvingly quoted Trump’s invocation of “gung-ho” as a symbol of Sino-US cooperation. The term originated in a wartime mistranslation of China’s Industrial Cooperatives (工合, for short) as “work together”, and a similar linguistic elasticity appears in Yuyuan Tantian’s treatment of “respect, fairness and reciprocity” (the US addition to the new formula of a “constructive relationship of strategic stability”, which China has now also adopted). In Trump-administration terms, “fairness and reciprocity” usually refers to redressing unequal market access and global trade imbalances. The blog acknowledges this, but instead recasts the phrase in terms of sovereign equality, national status and China’s preferred principles of global governance. Read here
China’s Strategy for Promoting Non-Alignment in Southeast Asia | Xue Song (23 September)
Dr Xue Song argues that Sino-Indonesian relations under President Prabowo Subianto are becoming “more strategic and institutionalised”. Her evidence includes the inaugural Comprehensive Strategic Dialogue, the second foreign and defence ministers’ (2+2) meeting, a planned 2027-31 action plan and expanding defence cooperation, including through the Peace Garuda exercises. She contends that economic frictions such as nickel policy can be contained within this framework, and that Indonesia’s engagement may widen political space for other ASEAN states to pursue defence ties with China. The institutional intensity is real and is broadening the relationship beyond economics. However, it also reflects a practical need to manage divergence, and both dynamics are at work. Read here
What China Wants from the Washington Summit (18 September)
The framing of “constructive strategic stability” has remained consistent since our coverage of the consensus view in May. “Strategic stability” is presented by many scholars as a consequence of “strategic stalemate”, a term that the IR scholar Jin Canrong has previously explained as emerging from Mao’s On Protracted War. It refers to temporary stability achieved through mutual deterrence, and in this case is widely seen as having been attained as the outcome of improvements in China’s relative strength. The “constructive relationship” part is more aspirational and is how Chinese scholars often distinguish this paradigm from the nuclear-deterrent-based “strategic stability” between the US and the Soviet Union. Read here
What China Needs from an AI Deal with America | Huang Ping (13 September)
AI is expected to be a central issue at the Xi-Trump summit later this September, but the scope for concessions on either side seems much less certain. US rhetoric around AI safety is often viewed sceptically in China as a means of holding back homegrown companies, and given the recent exchange of barbs between the US and China over AI distillation, the scope for agreement over the terms of market competition appears even narrower. Huang Ping, a scholar at CUHK-Shenzhen, nevertheless lays out why it would be in China’s interests to seek a much broader AI agreement to secure its access to global markets and influence over standards. Read here
Who Pays for the New Economy? Economic Digest: August 2026 (8 September)
Overall expectations for the second half of 2026 are low among Chinese economists. This is partly a matter of policy—many would have preferred an unambiguous shift towards fiscal stimulus after the mid-year Politburo meeting, which instead focused on incremental policies and accelerating the transition to “new growth drivers”. Yet, as Wu Ge argues, the fundamental macroeconomic direction is dictated less by policy than structural factors. Mainly, these are the deepening deflationary effects of local-government deleveraging as formerly hidden debts from local-government financing vehicles (LGFVs) are moved onto government balance sheets through debt swaps. Read here
China’s Mandate to Rule the Waves and Secure the Future | Di Dongsheng (3 September)
There is something distinctly High Victorian about Di Dongsheng’s closing proclamation that “the descendants of the dragon shall ultimately rule the stars and the waves”. Indeed, the piece certainly strikes an extremely hawkish tone throughout, with Di proposing the establishment of a naval–merchant–financial complex to wrest maritime power from the “Anglo Saxons”. Yet Di is also picking up on a familiar thread in Chinese strategic thinking, made newly urgent by events around the Strait of Hormuz: the vulnerability and importance of maritime chokepoints. Read here
Changes Unseen, Strategies Uncharted | Digest: August 2026 (31 August)
This month’s digest pulls in different directions—insofar as we can follow a single thread, it is that of traditional systems being swept away and of “changes unseen in a century” coming to pass: in discussions of nuclear proliferation, the Cold War nuclear order has “irreversibly come to an end”; in the Middle East, the US security architecture is crumbling; in the maritime domain, volatility threatens sea lanes; and overseas, Chinese firms’ modus operandi is shifting. While most scholars identify the increasing security risks attendant on such changes, what comes next and what China should do about it are open questions. More hawkish scholars advocate stronger unilateral action in the international system, while others caution against such measures. Read here
N.B. Sinification features a broad spectrum of voices, ranging from conservative hawks and state propagandists to more moderate and liberal thinkers. Readers are encouraged to bear this diversity in mind when engaging with the content.

articles.title: Reclinker raises £10m to turn demolition waste back into cement
articles.author: Cristian Dina
articles.content:
Reclinker, a startup that turns demolition waste back into cement, has raised £10m in a Series A round. It will use the money to move from trials to full commercial production in Cardiff. The company said on Monday that its process cuts cement’s emissions in half, at the same cost as conventional cement.
Clean Growth Fund and AP Ventures co-led the round. The Development Bank of Wales and Kibo Invest joined, along with existing investors Zero Carbon Capital and Cambridge Enterprise. Chief executive Bill Yost said the round was oversubscribed.
“This oversubscribed round sends a strong signal that UK investors are serious about decarbonisation,” Yost said.
Cement without a kiln
Cement causes about 7% of global CO₂ emissions, roughly three times as much as aviation, according to Reclinker. Most of it comes from making clinker, cement’s key ingredient. Kilns heat limestone, which releases CO₂ from the rock and from the fossil fuels that fire the kilns.
Researchers at the University of Cambridge developed Reclinker’s process and described it in a 2024 paper in Nature. It recovers old cement paste from demolished buildings. That paste then goes into the electric arc furnaces that already recycle scrap steel, where it turns back into clinker.
The furnace makes recycled steel and new cement at the same time. The process needs no kiln, no quarried limestone and no fossil-fuel heat. Reclinker expects a 50% cut in emissions at first, and more as the technology scales. TNW has not independently verified these figures.
Other heavy industries are also recycling their own waste into new material. Porsche has built a battery cell with a recycled cathode, made from its own old packs.
From trials to sales
Reclinker has made thousands of tonnes of its product at 7 Steel UK’s plant in Cardiff. It has also secured its first commercial sales. It targets a gap in supply. Concrete makers have long used blast-furnace slag for low-carbon cement blends. That slag is running out as steelmakers move away from blast furnaces.
“By investing alongside specialist climate technology investors, we’re helping Reclinker establish and grow its presence here,” said Gareth Mayhead of the Development Bank of Wales.
Through the Innovate UK Advance Market Commitment, large concrete users have said they plan to use more low-carbon materials. They aim to do so over the next five years. Beyond Cardiff, the money will help Reclinker take its process to other electric arc furnace sites in Europe and the US.
Construction technology has drawn large rounds this autumn. SoftBank invested $225m in autonomous construction firm ASI in September, a month after Gravis Robotics raised a $200m Series A led by SoftBank.
“Cement is one of the most challenging sectors to decarbonise, with emissions deeply embedded in both process chemistry and energy use,” said Stephen Price, investment partner at Clean Growth Fund.

Construction startup Reclinker has secured £10 million in Series A funding to scale its innovative process for recycling demolition waste into low-carbon cement at commercial production facilities.

### Key Points
- Reclinker raised £10 million in a round co-led by Clean Growth Fund and AP Ventures to expand operations from Cardiff to Europe and the US.
- The company’s technology, developed at the University of Cambridge, uses electric arc furnaces to convert demolition waste into cement without requiring traditional kilns.
- The process aims to reduce cement-related carbon emissions by 50% while maintaining cost parity with conventional manufacturing methods.
- Reclinker has already produced thousands of tonnes of material at a Celsa Steel UK plant and secured its first commercial sales contracts.
- The funding round included participation from the Development Bank of Wales, Kibo Invest, Zero Carbon Capital, and Cambridge Enterprise.

### Why it Matters
Cement production accounts for approximately 7% of global CO2 emissions, making it a critical target for industrial decarbonization efforts. By repurposing demolition waste, Reclinker offers a scalable solution to replace dwindling supplies of blast-furnace slag and helps the construction industry meet rising demand for sustainable building materials.

articles.title: AWS Client VPN now supports device posture assessment
articles.author: aws@amazon.com
articles.content:
AWS Client VPN now supports device posture assessment
AWS Client VPN now supports device posture assessment, allowing you to verify that connecting user devices meet your security and compliance requirements before granting network access. This feature integrates with your existing device posture providers, so only trusted, compliant devices can access your AWS resources through Client VPN.
Previously, Client VPN authenticated users through certificates, SAML, or Active Directory. With device posture assessment, you can now also integrate CrowdStrike , Jamf , or JumpCloud with Client VPN to automatically evaluate device security signals such as compliance scores, encryption status, and risk level before allowing a connection. You define these requirements using Cedar policies , giving you fine-grained control over which devices can connect. To help you author and validate these policies, Client VPN provides you a Test Policy tool that guides you through creating Cedar policies for your device posture requirements.
This feature continuously re-evaluates device compliance during active sessions, and automatically disconnects a session if a device falls out of compliance, such as when risk score or security settings change. You can also use this feature in monitoring-only mode, which logs posture evaluation results without disconnecting sessions, so you can assess the impact of your policies before enforcing them. Device posture assessment works alongside your existing authorization rules to provide defense in depth.
This feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Client VPN is available, at no additional cost. This feature requires AWS VPN Client version 6.2.0 or later.
To learn more about Client VPN:
- Visit the AWS Client VPN product page
- Download the AWS VPN Client
- Read the AWS Client VPN administrator guide
- Read the AWS Client VPN user guide
